subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 55-year-old man has a well-differentiated neoplasm composed of cells with neurosecretory granules. The pathologist notes that the tumor cells share amine precursor uptake and decarboxylase activity with cells in several different organs. She reviews the list of classic neuroendocrine neoplasms with her resident.
question: Which of the following is a classic neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas?

options.text: Carcinoid tumor
Small cell lung carcinoma
Medullary thyroid carcinoma
Pheochromocytoma
Insulinoma

explanation_correct: Neuroendocrine tumors are a heterogeneous group of neoplasms arising from neuroendocrine cells, which have features of both nerve cells and hormone-producing cells. They occur most often in the GI tract (carcinoid, gastrinoma), pancreas (insulinoma, glucagonoma), and lungs (small cell carcinoma), as well as the thyroid (medullary carcinoma) and adrenals (pheochromocytoma). Insulinoma is a tumor of pancreatic beta cells that overproduces insulin and causes hypoglycemia. All of the other listed tumors are also neuroendocrine, but at different anatomic sites.

explanation_incorrect.A: Carcinoid tumors are neuroendocrine neoplasms of the GI system, arising from enterochromaffin cells, not from the pancreas.
explanation_incorrect.B: Small cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor of the lung, not of the pancreas.
explanation_incorrect.C: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor derived from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid.
explanation_incorrect.D: Pheochromocytoma is a neuroendocrine tumor of adrenal chromaffin cells, not a pancreatic neoplasm.

educationalObjective: Neuroendocrine tumors arise at several sites; insulinoma is the classic pancreatic example, alongside GI carcinoid and gastrinoma.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 47-year-old woman has a midgut mass. Immunohistochemistry is positive for chromogranin A and neuron-specific enolase, and the tumor cells take up amine precursors and decarboxylate them. Despite their different embryologic origins, the pathologist notes that pancreatic beta cells and enterochromaffin cells behave similarly.
question: Which of the following best describes the shared property that links this tumor to pancreatic beta cells and enterochromaffin cells?

options.text: A common embryologic origin from neural crest cells
Amine precursor uptake and decarboxylase (APUD) activity with shared markers such as chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and NSE
Secretion of calcitonin as the common hormone product of all these cells
Origin from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland
A requirement for somatostatin to support tumor growth

explanation_correct: Neuroendocrine cells share a common biologic function through amine precursor uptake and decarboxylase (APUD) activity, despite differences in embryologic origin, anatomic site, and secretory products. They express characteristic markers including chromogranin A, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), synaptophysin, serotonin, histamine, and calcitonin. This functional concept unifies tumors as diverse as carcinoid, insulinoma, small cell lung carcinoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma. Treatment is surgical resection and somatostatin analogs.

explanation_incorrect.A: APUD cells have differing embryologic origins; the shared feature is functional, not a common neural crest lineage.
explanation_incorrect.C: Calcitonin is the specific product of thyroid medullary C cells, not a universal product of all APUD cells.
explanation_incorrect.D: Parafollicular C cells are thyroid-specific; this patient's tumor arises in the midgut.
explanation_incorrect.E: Somatostatin analogs are used as treatment to suppress secretion; they are not a growth requirement for these tumors.

educationalObjective: APUD activity and shared immunohistochemical markers (chromogranin A, synaptophysin, NSE) define the neuroendocrine cell family.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 3-year-old child is brought in with progressive abdominal distension. Palpation reveals a firm, irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline. Urinary catecholamine metabolites are elevated, and blood pressure is normal. The parents ask why this is not the more common kidney tumor of childhood.
question: Which of the following findings best supports neuroblastoma over Wilms tumor in this child?

options.text: Episodic hypertension from catecholamine excess, as is typical of neuroblastoma
A smooth, unilateral flank mass that does not cross the midline
A firm, irregular mass that crosses the midline with elevated urinary HVA and VMA
A first-degree relative with familial Wilms tumor
Presentation after age 10 with normal urinary catecholamine metabolites

explanation_correct: Neuroblastoma is the most common solid extracranial tumor of childhood, typically affecting children under 4 years old. It arises from neural crest cells, usually in the adrenal medulla or along the sympathetic chain. Its classic presentation is abdominal distension with a firm, irregular mass that crosses the midline, in contrast to the smooth, unilateral flank mass of Wilms tumor. Urinary HVA and VMA are elevated, and the tumor is usually normotensive, unlike pheochromocytoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neuroblastoma is usually normotensive; episodic hypertension is characteristic of pheochromocytoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: A smooth, unilateral flank mass is the classic description of Wilms tumor, not neuroblastoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: A family history of Wilms tumor would support Wilms tumor and does not explain elevated catecholamine metabolites.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neuroblastoma typically presents before age 4 and is associated with elevated, not normal, urinary HVA and VMA.

educationalObjective: A firm irregular midline-crossing abdominal mass with elevated urine HVA/VMA in a young child distinguishes neuroblastoma from Wilms tumor.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 2-year-old has an abdominal mass. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells arranged around a central fibrillary area of neuropil. Cytogenetic analysis demonstrates amplification of a gene encoding a transcription factor, and the tumor stains strongly for neuron-specific enolase and bombesin.
question: Which of the following findings is most characteristic of this tumor?

options.text: Homer-Wright rosettes and N-myc oncogene amplification
Psammoma bodies and activating RET point mutations
Schiller-Duval bodies and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein
Reinke crystals and androgen secretion
Verocay bodies and Antoni A areas

explanation_correct: The biopsy shows Homer-Wright rosettes — neuroblasts surrounding a central area of neuropil — which are characteristic of neuroblastoma (and also medulloblastoma). Neuroblastoma is a neural crest–derived tumor with amplification of the N-myc oncogene, increased urinary HVA and VMA, and elevated bombesin and NSE. These features, together with the patient's age and adrenal or sympathetic chain location, confirm the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Psammoma-like calcifications and RET mutations point toward medullary thyroid carcinoma; neuroblastoma is defined by N-myc amplification.
explanation_incorrect.C: Schiller-Duval bodies with elevated alpha-fetoprotein are features of yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor, a germ cell neoplasm.
explanation_incorrect.D: Reinke crystals are found in Leydig cell tumors of the testis, not in neural crest tumors.
explanation_incorrect.E: Verocay bodies and Antoni A areas are histologic hallmarks of schwannoma, a benign nerve sheath tumor.

educationalObjective: Homer-Wright rosettes and N-myc amplification are the signature histologic and genetic findings of neuroblastoma.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 58-year-old man has a well-differentiated gastrinoma with several small liver metastases. The oncology team discusses therapy aimed at controlling hormone secretion and limiting tumor burden, in addition to considering surgical options.
question: Which of the following is the standard treatment approach for neuroendocrine tumors?

options.text: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement therapy
Radioactive iodine (131I) ablation
BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibition
Surgical resection and somatostatin analogs
Thyrotropin-suppressive levothyroxine

explanation_correct: The mainstay of treatment for neuroendocrine tumors is surgical resection when feasible, with somatostatin analogs used to suppress hormone secretion and control symptoms, particularly in unresectable or metastatic disease. This approach applies across the spectrum of neuroendocrine neoplasms, including gastrinoma, carcinoid, and insulinoma. Somatostatin analogs reduce secretion from APUD cells, addressing the hormonal manifestations of these tumors.

explanation_incorrect.A: Glucocorticoid replacement treats adrenal insufficiency; it has no role as primary therapy for neuroendocrine tumors.
explanation_incorrect.B: Radioiodine ablates thyroid follicular tissue; neuroendocrine tumors do not concentrate iodine.
explanation_incorrect.C: BCR-ABL inhibition is targeted therapy for chronic myeloid leukemia, not for neuroendocrine neoplasms.
explanation_incorrect.E: TSH-suppressive levothyroxine is used in differentiated thyroid cancer, not in gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

educationalObjective: Neuroendocrine tumors are treated with surgical resection plus somatostatin analogs to control tumor growth and hormone secretion.
